version_history.subject: [RFC PATCH 0/1] mm/swap: keep reclaim batches contiguous on swap

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/1] mm/swap: allocate contiguous swap slots for a reclaim batch
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes swap slot allocation by allocating contiguous slots in batches, reducing the number of small write requests and improving performance. It achieves this by recording the number of pages of each order that need a slot before swapping out a batch, and then making those allocations follow contiguous free slots. This approach helps to minimize the fragmentation of swap clusters and reduces the overhead of small write requests.

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns that the patch does not address workloads that benefit more from disk swapping than compression swapping, and requested further consideration for these use cases.

Reviewer noted that the patch does not apply its contiguous allocation heuristic to folios larger than a certain order, and found this omission reasonable.

Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concern that the patch's preference for non-full clusters with contiguous slots may lead to increased lock contention, especially as swapfiles become more fragmented.

Reviewer Nhat Pham raised concerns about the effectiveness of the contiguous swap slot allocation heuristic, questioning whether it would lead to overshooting the estimate and creating problems down the line. They also suggested that this heuristic might not be necessary for cgroups that enable zswap or zram.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks for looking into this! There are still workloads that benefit
more from disk swapping than compression swapping... We should make
the swap subsystem work for them.

I haven't read the code too closely, as it's an RFC meant to show the
general idea. So I'll just make some comments and ask some questions
about the idea:

---

Ah so we don't invoke this heuristics for folio larger than certain
orders? Makes sense.

---

So we prefer non-full clusters with contiguous slots, over free
clusters, over other nonfull clusters.

I think this part makes sense to me FWIW. We do skip fast path and go
for slow paths more often, so do make sure we're not paying with too
much lock contention, especially as the swapfile fils or get more
fragmented (which this patch series does nudge us towards). But FWIW,
we pretty much go back to the old behavior the moment we fail to find
contiguity for the first time in the batch, so I think we'll be
fine...?

---

Some general questions:

1. How many pages in folio_list typically do get reclaimed? There can
be quite a few with references, which we rotate/promote, when we scan,
right? Would constantly overshooting the estimate create problem down
the line?

(This is one of the few places where indirection (vswap) would have
helped - we can collect a batch of pages after unmapping, then pass
them to the phys swap allocator (after checking zswappability, etc.).
Maybe we can solve it better after it's landed, and accept an
imperfect solution for now?)

2. Should we skip this heuristics for cgroups that enables zswap (and
maybe zram)? Contiguity matters less there... unless it help at
writeback time? Hard to say without experimentation - maybe you can do
the same check you did for your zswap writeback batching patch series?

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch aims to reduce the number of I/O requests on a swap device by keeping reclaim batches contiguous. The current implementation of swap allocation and deallocation can lead to scattered writes, resulting in increased I/O requests. The patch modifies the allocator to allocate contiguous free slots for a reclaim batch, reducing the number of small requests and improving throughput. This is achieved by informing the allocator about the size of the batch and allowing it to allocate contiguous slots accordingly. The goal is to reduce the overhead of swap I/O operations and improve system performance.

review_comments.author: Kairui Song
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Kairui Song suggested reverting commit 9a42aed48421, which prefers nonfull over free clusters for small order allocations, and instead always scanning full clusters to prioritize contiguity on large physical swap devices.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hi Alexandre,

That's a interesting problem. I think the real problem is with commit
9a42aed48421 ("mm, swap: prefer nonfull over free clusters"), right?

It's more like a balance between fragmentation and contiguity of small
order allocation issue.

Perhaps we should instead always scan the full clusters and revert
that one commit? That commit was only following the idea of keeping
the allocation more compacted for that series, it looked good at that
time. Since fragmentation issues can be solved in other ways,
contiguity seems to matter more for large physical swap devices.

What are the other fragmentation solutions you are referring to?

Alex

review_comments.author: Nhat Pham
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Nhat Pham expressed concerns that the proposed solution of allocating contiguous swap slots may not address the underlying issue and could lead to increased memory overhead, scanning overhead, etc., suggesting that physical swap space compaction is still a problem and virtual swap space would just shift the issue.
review_comments.raw_body:
Hmm what other way are you thinking of? Physical swap space compaction
requires vswap, which has not landed. And we'd just be kicking the
problem to virtual swap space. Sure, we won't be failing allocation,
but that would still increase the memory overhead, scanning overhead,
etc.

I encountered this myself. Remember when I wrote my own swap allocator
for vswap? In one of the version, I went for free clusters first
instead of partial clusters. It fragmented the swap space, so I had to
copy your homework and went for partially used clusters first...

Anyway, maybe I'm wrong - some numbers would be nice here.

review_comments.author: Kairui Song
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer suggested limiting the patch's scope to SYNC devices or exploring simpler solutions to address the problem, expressing skepticism about the significance of a 4% reduction in mTHP failures.

Reviewer Kairui Song suggested addressing swap space fragmentation by sorting clusters by slot size before moving them back to the non-full list, which would mitigate the issue until a more comprehensive solution is implemented.
review_comments.raw_body:
That patch is 1/3 of a series, that series yields really nice
results, but that one patch plays only a small part in them. Or
perhaps we can limit that to SYNC devices? I hope there are simpler
ways to avoid the problem you encountered. I think the ~4% reduction
of 64k mTHP failure is kind of trivial compared to the problem you
encountered, and 2M swapout is still not easily doable, as the
main blocker is from the page allocator.

Right, nothing has landed in upstream for that yet, but with larger

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm/mempolicy: recompute automatic interleave weights on memory hotplug

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/mempolicy: recompute automatic interleave weights on memory hotplug

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch updates the automatic interleave weights in Linux's memory policy when a node gains or loses memory due to hotplug events. The current implementation only recalculates the weights when a new bandwidth is reported, which can lead to incorrect weights being used for some nodes. This patch introduces a new function `wi_state_refresh` that recomputes the weights from the recorded bandwidth whenever a node gains its first memory or loses its last. This ensures that the weighted interleave algorithm always uses accurate and up-to-date weights, leading to improved performance in certain scenarios.

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm/vmscan: reclaim every zone in per-node proactive reclaim

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the per-node proactive reclaim function to scan every zone, not just ZONE_NORMAL, in order to reclaim movable memory as well. This addresses a problem where nodes with only movable memory were not being reclaimed properly. The approach taken is to change the `reclaim_idx` field of the `scan_control` structure to always set it to the maximum number of zones, allowing all zones to be scanned.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/2] memcg: reduce cacheline contention between lruvec stat updates and LRU lists
series_items.patch_summary: This patch reduces cacheline contention between lruvec stat updates and LRU lists by rearranging the layout of struct mem_cgroup_per_node in memory. The goal is to minimize unnecessary overhead caused by spatial prefetching on Intel CPUs, which can lead to increased lock contention and slower performance. The patch achieves this by moving the 'memcg_pn_cold' group after 'memcg_pn_read_mostly', ensuring that the read-mostly cacheline is paired with the cold cacheline instead of the LRU list heads. This change was validated through benchmarking, which showed a significant reduction in contention and improved performance.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/2] memcg: don't go through the lruvec for folio and kmem lruvec stat updates
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes memory cgroup (memcg) statistics updates by bypassing the lruvec data structure for folio and kmem lruvec stat updates. It directly passes the memcg and node to the mod_memcg_node_state function, reducing contention with other threads that access the lru_lock holder. This change improves throughput in certain scenarios, such as on a 2-socket Skylake system with multiple threads accessing shared memory.

review_comments.author: Michal Hocko
review_comments.summary: Gave Acked-by

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch reduces cacheline contention between lruvec stat updates and LRU lists by rearranging the layout of struct mem_cgroup_per_node to pair read-mostly lines with cold lines, and modifying folio and kmem stat updates to avoid going through the lruvec. This change improves performance on systems that use spatial prefetching, such as Intel CPUs. The patch includes two changes: one that reorders the fields in struct mem_cgroup_per_node, and another that modifies the stat update functions to skip using the lruvec. The results show a significant improvement in pages per second for threads faulting in and freeing memory in a single memcg.

review_comments.author: Andrew Morton
review_comments.summary: The reviewer noted that even though the patch rearranges struct mem_cgroup_per_node to pair its read-mostly line with a cold line, it does not guarantee that every read-mostly line will be paired with a cold line due to SLAB_HWCACHE_ALIGN slab usage, which can align objects to 128-byte boundaries but still allow adjacent objects to share a cacheline pair.
review_comments.raw_body:
Thanks.  A local AI review pointed out a thing:

  One limitation worth mentioning in the [1/2] changelog: the slab
  uses SLAB_HWCACHE_ALIGN, which need not align each object to a
  128-byte boundary.  If an object starts 64 bytes into such a pair,
  its first line can still be paired with the end of the preceding
  object rather than its own cold line.  This isn't a correctness
  issue, and the measured Skylake improvement may well be real, but the
  layout doesn't guarantee that every read-mostly line pairs with a
  cold line.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 1/5] mm/memcontrol: flatten try_charge_memcg control flow
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the try_charge_memcg function in mm/memcontrol.c to simplify its control flow by separating the logic for memsw and memory page counters into distinct paths. This makes it easier to follow the code, especially after making page_counter_try_charge stock-aware. The change does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 2/5] mm/page_counter: introduce per-CPU stock
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a per-CPU stock representation in the page_counter layer, similar to memcg's seven-slot per-CPU stock. It adds a new struct page_counter_stock_pcp that preserves the existing behavior from memcg and includes a backpointer to the base of the percpu stock. The patch also updates the page_counter structure to include pointers to the percpu stock and its owning cgroup_subsys_state. No functional changes are intended in this patch, which is part of a larger series.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 3/5] mm/page_counter: make page_counter_try_charge() stock-aware
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the page_counter_try_charge() function to be aware of stock, allowing it to consume stock transparently while preserving existing semantics. Two new parameters are added: may_batch and nr_charged. The first parameter preserves the behavior of !allow_spinning scenarios in try_charge_memcg, where charges are made as quickly as possible without evicting other stock slots or making a greedy charge to refill the stock. The second parameter reflects the size of the successful hierarchy charge, preserving batch-based memory.high accounting for current->memcg_nr_pages_over_high.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 4/5] mm/memcontrol: move memory stock to page counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch moves the memory stock from memcg to page counters, allowing for more efficient management of memory usage. The change affects how memory and swap counters interact, potentially causing temporary divergence in their raw values. To maintain compatibility, the patch introduces a new logic to ensure that reclaim doesn't swap when memory fails first, even if memory and swap have equal limits. The patch also removes unused memcg code and preserves existing behaviors for cgroup v2 users. The change sets the stage for future work on introducing additional page counters without breaking the fast path.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v7 5/5] mm/memcontrol: add stock to the memsw page counter
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a separate stock to the memsw page counter, allowing it to operate independently of the memory bank. The common drain scheduling is factored into schedule_stock_drain(), which handles charge, refill, and hotplug operations for both stocks. If memory charge fails, only nr_pages from memsw are rolled back. The patch also preserves the user-visible cgroup-v1 memory invariant by reporting memory.usage_in_bytes as the smaller raw value.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series moves the stock management from mem_cgroup to page_counter, allowing each page_counter to have its own per-CPU cache of pre-charged pages. This change is necessary for future work on scalable and performant page_counters, such as the tiered memcg limits series. The decoupling of memory and memsw stocks in cgroup v1 users may lead to different sizes of precharged caches, but the patch preserves the invariant that memory.usage_in_bytes is less than or equal to memory.memsw.usage_in_bytes by reporting the smaller value. This change has no functional impact on memcg v2 users.

review_comments.summary:
The author is addressing concerns about the patch's impact on cgroupv2, specifically how it will interact with new page_counters being added to struct memcg. The author acknowledges that the current implementation of stocking charge for memcg is equivalent to stocking charge for the memcg->memory page_counter and explains that their ongoing work adds new per-tier page_counters to struct memcg, which cannot use the stock fastpath due to its inability to distinguish memory residence. They argue that their patch avoids hierarchy walks for most charges.

Author agrees that additional context is needed and plans to provide it by adding call traces, indicating that no fix is currently planned but more information will be provided.

Author addressed a concern about the impact of separate stocking on cgroup v1 users by explaining that memory.usage_in_bytes will be reported as the smaller of raw memory and memsw values to preserve the invariant.

Author acknowledged that cgroup v2 users should not see any changes in the patch series and offered to provide additional explanation on how stocking currently works.

The author is addressing concerns about the behavior of reporting memory usage when memsw and memory stocks are decoupled. He acknowledges that there can be an inversion where memsw reports a higher usage than memory, but explains that this is due to how direct charging works in such scenarios. The author proposes fuzzily reporting the minimum of the two reported values, which he claims aligns with the existing fuzzy nature of usage_in_bytes.
review_comments.raw_body:
So right now for cgroupv2, there's kind of a 1-1 mapping between
page_counter and memcg. I say "kind of" because there still is a
page_counter for swap, but it takes a completely different charging
path (i.e. not try_charge_memcg).

This means that currently stocking charge for memcg is equivalent to
stocking charge for the memcg->memory page_counter.

However, one of the series that I'm currently working on [1] adds new
page_counters to struct memcg to track the usage of memory
per-memcg, per-tier. The goal is to (1) track how much memory of a
cgroup lives on which tier, and (2) to limit the usage so that a single
cgroup doesn't use up all the fast tier memory alone, and shares it
fairly with all the other cgroups on the host.

When adding a new per-tier page_counter to struct mem_cgroup that gets
charged for every memcg_charge, I cannot use the stock fastpath since
the stock does not distinguish where the memory resides. It would
essentialy boil down to this pattern:

try_charge_memcg
   \__ page_couner_try_charge(memcg->tier[0])
   \__ consume_stock()

Where every path still has to do a hierarchy charge to the tier it's
charging to, whereas this patch gets us:

try_charge_memcg
   \__ page_counter_try_charge(memcg->tier[0])
          \__ consume_stock(memcg->tier[0])
   \__ page_countertry_charge(memcg->memory)
          \__ consume_stock(memcg->memory)

So that we can avoid the hierarchy walk for most charges.

I'd be happy to submit a new cover letter which better explains this
idea!

---

Sounds good with me. I can add the call traces above which should
explain my thought process a bit more. Hopefully the problem I am
trying to solve is evident there.

---

No changes to locking. In fact this series is mostly just moving code
from mm/memcontrol.c to mm/page_counter.c, everything is essentially
the same.

---

This series should not have any changes for cgroup v2, including when
and where the cache is stocked / drained in the hierarchy. I can
include a snippet on how stocking currently works to add a visual
explanation, if that helps too.

---

Yeah, so this part is a little bit annoying. Let's just look at a single
leaf cgroup for example, where the limit for memsw and memory are both
64 pages.

charge_memcg(64)
	raw memory: 64			raw memsw: 64
	reported memory: 64		reported memsw: 64
	memory stock: 0			memory stock: 0

swap out 32 pages
	raw memory: 32			raw memsw: 64
	reported memory: 32		reported memsw: 64
	memory stock: 0			memsw stock: 0

free 32 pages
	raw memory: 0			raw memsw: 32
	reported memory: 0		reported memsw: 32
	memory stock: 0			memsw stock: 0

charge_memcg(1)
	raw memory: 1			raw memsw: 33
	reported memory: 64		reported memsw: 33
	memory stock: 63		memsw stock: 0

Where the last charge_memcg() causes the inversion. memsw tries to
charge a batch of 64 to refill the stock, but fails since 32+64=96
puts the memsw over its max limit. So it falls back to direct charging
where it charges the page_counter directly, and ends up with 0 stock
and reporting a usage of 33.

On the other hand, memory will greedily refill the stock with 64 pages
and since usage is 0, the batch refill will succeed, and it will report
a usage of 64.

So the idea with reporting the minimum is to report the minimum of the
two reported values, we will just fuzzily report the stocked value.
IIRC usage_in_bytes has always been fuzzy anyways, due to how much
memory has been stocked.

Thanks again for taking a look, Michal! I hope you have a great day : -)
Joshua
